hook.en: A radio station talks and you only listen. On a walkie-talkie you take turns. On a phone call you can both talk at once. These are three types of *communication*.

title.en: Compare circuit switching and packet switching

say.en: A radio station talks and you only listen. On a walkie-talkie you take turns. On a phone call you can both talk at once. These are three types of communication. In this lesson: Distinguish simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex.
Compare circuit switching and packet switching.

body.en: *Simplex*: data flows in only one direction, e.g. keyboard to computer, radio or TV broadcast. Half-duplex: data flows in both directions but only one direction at a time, e.g. walkie-talkie. Full-duplex: data flows in both directions at the same time, e.g. a telephone or video call.

title.en: On the board: Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex, and switching

say.en: Simplex: data flows one way only, like a keyboard to a computer or a TV broadcast.
Half-duplex: both ways, but only one way at a time, like a walkie-talkie.
Full-duplex: both ways at the same time, like a telephone call.
In circuit switching, one dedicated path is reserved for the whole call, as in an old landline.
In packet switching, the message is split into numbered packets. Each may take a different route, and the receiver puts them back in order.

body.en: Switching decides how data moves through a network of many nodes. In *circuit switching*, a dedicated path is set up between sender and receiver before communication and is held for the whole session, as in a traditional landline call. In packet switching, the message is broken into packets; each packet carries the destination address, may take a different route, and the packets are reassembled in order at the destination. The Internet uses packet switching.

points.en: *Packet*: no dedicated path; packets routed independently

narration.en: Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path for the whole call. Packet switching breaks data into packets that may take different routes, as on the Internet.

problem.en: Classify each: (i) a cricket commentary on FM radio, (ii) a police wireless handset, (iii) an online class where students and teacher talk freely, (iv) a printer receiving a document from a computer that never replies.

steps.en: (ii) Press-to-talk, one side at a time → half-duplex.
(iii) Both talk and listen together → full-duplex.
(iv) Data in one direction only → simplex (as stated in the problem).

narration.en: Let us work through this together. Classify each: (i) a cricket commentary on FM radio, (ii) a police wireless handset, (iii) an online class where students and teacher talk freely, (iv) a printer receiving a document from a computer that never replies.

say.en: Let us work through this together. Classify each: i a cricket commentary on FM radio, ii a police wireless handset, iii an online class where students and teacher talk freely, iv a printer receiving a document from a computer that never replies.
i Listeners cannot reply gives simplex.
ii Press-to-talk, one side at a time gives half-duplex.
iii Both talk and listen together gives full-duplex.
iv Data in one direction only gives simplex as stated in the problem.
So the answer is i simplex, ii half-duplex, iii full-duplex, iv simplex.

say.en: Pause and solve this exam pattern question. How long does it take to transfer a 20 MB file over a link with a data transfer rate of 4 Mbps? (Take 1 byte equals 8 bits.).
20 MB equals 20 times 8 equals 160 megabits.
Time equals 160 Mb divided by 4 Mbps equals 40 seconds.
5 seconds forgets to convert bytes to bits.
